speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. In Hansard of Friday last I observe, at page 3079, that some remarks were made by the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart), which remarks directly concern myself. They have to do with the occurrences at a convention held at the city of Hamilton the night before. The report in connection with which the hon. member spoke is not identified, but purports to come from Hamilton under date of June 25. In order that I may identify what I have to say, perhaps the house will bear with me while I quote that report. It reads as follows:
Charges that four cabinet ministers in the recent Liberal government at Ottawa had promised to smash the glass industry in Hamilton were levelled by C. W. Bell, K.C., M.P. for Hamilton West, addressing the Conservative convention here to-night in the federal riding of Hamilton East at which M. M. Robinson, sportsman and newspaperman, was chosen Conservative candidate to contest the riding at the by-election, August 10.
Hon. Charles Stewart, Minister of the Interior, and Hon. James Malcolm, Minister of Trade and Commerce in the King government, and two other cabinet ministers had opposed the efforts of Hamilton to build up the glass industry there, said Mr. Bell.
Referring to his efforts to aid glass manufacturers in the city, Mr. Bell said: "This is the truth of the thing.
The report then continues, "In ten or twelve visits," and then follows in parantheses "to

Privilege-Mr. Bell (Hamilton)
government officials at Ottawa"; this is distinctly inaccurate as these visits were made to Ottawa amongst other places. The report continues :
I did all I could. Yet every time I went to them I found that a new flood of propaganda undermining the confidence of their financial backers had been poured upon them.
This went on until one day at Ottawa I was told by Mr. Stewart, the Minister of the Interior in the King administration, and Mr. Malcolm, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and two other cabinet ministers that they would never let Hamilton get its glass industry. And they said: 'We will smash your d- industry.' "
The hon. member for Antigonish-Guysboro (Mr. Duff) then interjected, "That means ' damned,' " which proves my contention that he and I speak the same language. The hon. member for West Edmonton then continued:
May I say that when a member of the government I never was canvassed by the hon. member for West Hamilton (Mr. Bell) for aid for the glass industry.
There are points on which I disagree with my hon. friend, and those points I propose to mention presently. However, let me say that so far as that statement is concerned, I agree cordially with him; he never was canvassed by me for aid for the glass industry whilst he was a member of the recent government, nor did I ever say so. In so far as this statement, whatever its source may be, relates to the hon. members for West Edmonton and North Bruce (Mr. Malcolm), to that extent it is entirely accurate. The hon. member for West Edmonton continued:
When the present government cancelled by an order in council the duty which was imposed at the September session, I met the hon. member in the Chateau Laurler and had a discussion with him, but that is the only conversation I have had with him with respect to this matter.
Then the hon. member for North Bruce, in his invariably fair manner, said:
Mr. Speaker, may I join with the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) in saying that I do not wish to doubt the accuracy of the report, but as it is not based on any conversation that I can recall, I am inclined to think that the statement attributed to the hon. member for West Hamilton is not in accordance with the facts.
Under the circumstances which then obtained, I can quite believe that this matter might easily have passed from the minds of both hon. members in question, but it did not pass from mine. The circumstances to which I allude have to do not with the occasion when the glass tariff had been recalled or cancelled, but rather with an occasion some weeks after the breakup of the emergency session in September. At that time the

criticisms which were being made publicly of the efforts to establish industries amounted to a very distinct newspaper propaganda. I made a number of visits to Ottawa, as I made visits elsewhere, in an endeavour to get this industry on its feet. On the occasion to which I am referring I met the hon. members for West Edmonton and North Bruce in the Chateau Laurier. I was sending a telegram and was standing at the stand where telegrams are written, and my hon. friends came along. The hon. member for West Edmonton stood at the end of the stand, and the hon. member for North Bruce stood up against the counter where the telegrams are accepted. Both hon. members started to chaff me about our inability to get going, and presently the hon. member for North Bruce said, "Charlie, you might as well go home, you cannot do anything here; you will never get your glass factory opened." I said, "If you fellows would only leave us alone we could get it opened, but it is this ceaseless, everyday propaganda which is blocking us and we cannot get anywhere." The hon. member for West Edmonton then laughed as he is laughing now, only perhaps a little more heartily.
I do not blame him.

I am not asking
the opinion of the hon. member. The hon. member for West Edmonton then said to me, "That is right, Charlie, we are going to smash that glass tariff of yours if it is the last thing we do."
What about the "damn"?

That is just what would occur to the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysboro. Then both my hon. friends laughed and went away.
I could not laugh, Mr. Speaker, because my thoughts were with the unfortunate people in Hamilton, the poor, the needy and the unemployed who were out of work and who were looking for a chance to obtain employment through the establishment of this industry; I could not laugh at that although it seemed so funny to my hon. friends. From the attitude taken by hon. members opposite, I can quite believe that-

I must ask the hon.
member to confine himself to a statement of what occurred. He is replying to a statement concerning himself which was made in this house, and I must ask him to confine himself to a statement of the facts.

Naturally, at that time the circumstances were such that the words uttered by my hon. friends burned

Privilege-Mr. Bell (Hamilton)
themselves into my memory. There is no mistake about those words being uttered in the way in which they were, and that is what I want this house to appreciate and understand.
That is not all of it. Presumably after these statements were made in the house, my hon. friends gave an interview to that very excellent Liberal paper, The Hamilton Herald, and in its issue of Friday, June 26, on page 3, I read the following:
"The only time I ever discussed the glass industry of Hamilton with Mr. Bell," said Mr. Stewart, "was after the present Conservative government removed the high duties imposed at the special session of parliament last fall, and that night Mr. Bell was going to leave the Conservative party because of the government's action."
The next time the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr.Stewart) undertakes to correct me, he should get a little better acquainted with the facts. The house will notice the statement:
Removed the high duties imposed at the special session of parliament last fall, and that night-
The fact is that that night the hon. member for West Hamilton was in Cochrane, 480 miles away from the city of Ottawa. That is the exact circumstance and it shows the accuracy of my hon. friend's statement. All that week, beginning on Monday 6 and continuing until Friday 10, I was engaged at the assizes at Cochrane before Mr. Justice Garrow, and I was not any nearer Ottawa than 480 miles away. That sho-ws the accuracy of the statement made by the hon. member for West Edmonton.
Further, the hon. member for West Edmonton says:
-Mr. Bell was going to leave the Conservative party because of the government's action.
I never at any time made any such statement to him or to anyone else, and any time that I think of so acting, the first person to learn of it will be my right hon leader (Mr. Bennett) and not the hon. member for West Edmonton. I have before me the order in council dated the 9th day of October, 1930, when that tariff was removed. On that date the hon. member for Argenteuil (Sir George Perky) telephoned to me at Cochrane informing me of that removal. Therefore, at that time I was the distance I have stated from Ottawa. The hon. member for West Edmonton is totally, hopelessly inaccurate in his statement with regard to the events of that night; he cannot get away from that. I would not be so boorish as to attribute to my hon. friend the deliberate invention of any misstatement; I would not credit cr discredit
him with anything of that sort. So far as I am concerned, I believe every hon. member records the facts exactly as he believes them to be, but that statement to a newspaper is calculated to do me as grievous an injustice as could possibly be done to any man because it contains the allegation that I would be guilty of disloyalty to my leader and my party. It is absolutely incorrect and my hon. friend is entirely wrong in the thought to which he is reported as having given expression. I am quite willing to give him credit for being mistaken, but I repeat there is nothing correct in that statement which has been given out to the Hamilton Herald, and I ask now that the hon. member for West Edmonton disavow it or give me that withdrawal to which I am entitled.
What specific statement is the hon. member asking me to withdraw; he has made so many.
If my hon. friend had listened to me, he would not have had any difficulty in knowing.
If the hon. member will put his statement in definite terms, I will answer it.

My hon friend, as I have informed the house, is credited in the Hamilton Herald, the Liberal paper in that city, with having said:
"The only time I ever discussed the glass industry of Hamilton with Mr. Bell," said Mr. Stewart, "was after the present Conservative government removed the high duties imposed at the special session of parliament last fall, and that night Mr. Bell was going to leave the Conservative party because of the government's action."
I ask my hon. friend to disavow the entire paragraph which I have read or else give me the withdrawal to which I am entitled.

The reason I asked my hon. friend
to be specific about the statement was that the inference I drew, and the inference, I think, the house drew, was that this happened the night of the date of the order in council removing the duty on glass.
The statement says so.
It does not say so. I said it happened after the event and that statement is quite correct.

That is a fine
crawl 1

There is no crawl about it any more than my hon. friend

Privilege-Mr. Bell (Hamilton)
is seeking to crawl at the present moment. My hon. friend knows quite well the instance spoken of, which he made so much of the other night, is the result of the fact well known throughout Canada that I am known to be perhaps the low tariff member of the late government-it will go down better that way-and anything that happened that night was purely in the nature of a chaffing game.

Then my hon.
friend admits it.

I say now
on my responsibility as a member of the house that I never made the statement that I would smash the glass industry of Hamilton.

I say the hon.
member did.

I say I did
not. I say this on my responsibility as a member and I have just as much right to ask my hon. friend to withdraw his statement as he has to ask me to withdraw mine. I do not deny that I was opposed to an increase in the duty on glass; everyone knows that. I do not deny I was opposed to increases in the duties on almost every article contained in the budget of last September, but I do most emphatically deny that I would smash the glass industry of Hamilton, because I never uttered any such words. I think I have said enough to convince my hon. friend. I do not propose to have anything of that kind shoved down my throat.
Nor I, either.
Order.

Perhaps I
have gone too far and I will withdraw anything unparliamentary that I may have said in that regard, but I do not propose to rest under a statement never made by me on any occasion. 1 have not had many conversations with the hon. gentleman, and I am sure the hon. member for North Bruce (Mr. Malcolm) will bear me out, that no such statement was ever made.
Except chaffingly, as my hon. friend has just admitted.

Will the hon. member give
the names of the two cabinet ministers who were there?

The hon. member for
West Hamilton has addressed the house on a question of privilege. The hon. member for West Edmonton has replied. There is no debate.
On the orders of the day:

I rise to a question of privilege. I want to refer to a statement in the Toronto Globe under date of Friday last, June 26, in connection with the report of a speech that the hon. member for West Hamilton (Mr. Bell) made at a convention held in that city, at which convention a Conservative candidate was chosen for the by-election. According to the report, the hon. member for West Hamilton mentioned my name and that of another hon. member on this side. Without giving their names he referred to twelve other Liberal members. Before I read this report from the Toronto Globe, I should like to say that I am glad the hon. member for West Hamilton is in his seat to-day. He has not appeared in the house very often lately.
That comment is entirely unnecessary. If the hon. member has a question of privilege to state, I would ask him to state it.
I am coming to it.

Will the hon. member
state it now?

I bow to your ruling, Mr. Speaker. I read as follows from the Toronto Globe of June 26; it is headed "Laughs":
Mr. Bell referred to the charge of Mr. King that Premier Bennett had laughed. "Why, I can tell you that Hepburn, Sanderson and a dozen other Liberals laughed outright in the house several years ago when I told of the woe the then depression was causing in Hamilton. You will remember that scores of poor persons here gathered grass and twigs on the face of the mountain, because they had no other fuel. When I mentioned such distress it was then that Hepburn and the others laughed."
The hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Hepburn) is not in his seat; unfortunately he cannot be present. The hon. member for West Hamilton must have known, when he made that attack, that the hon. member for West Elgin was critically ill. I am sure the hon. member for West Elgin, if he were here-

Has the hon. member
anything to say relating to himself?
I have.
If he has, he has a right to proceed with it; otherwise I shall have to interrupt him and go on with the business of the house.

All right, I desire to
say, Mr. Speaker, that the speech to which

Privilege-Mr. Sanderson
the hon. member for West Hamilton refers was . made on February 2, 1926, and I propose before I take my seat to read part of that speech which he says the hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Hepburn) and myself laughed at. The speech in question was delivered on February 2, 1926, and I would point out to you, Mr. Speaker, and to hon. members of this house that the hon. member for West Elgin was not then a member of parliament. He was elected on September 14, 1926, and he took his seat on December 7, 1926, so obviously he could not have sat in this house and laughed at the hon. member for West Hamilton on February 2, 1926. Whether I laughed then or not, Mr. Speaker,
I am not prepared to say.

Then I think that should be sufficient. I cannot see that any question of privilege is involved in whether the hon. member laughed or not. I must call the 'hon. member to order. There is such a thing as going to extremes under the guise of personal privilege. I cannot see that this is worthy of the attention of the house on a question of privilege. Whether the hon. member laughed or not five years ago makes no difference, and I must call him to order.
Of necessity I must bow to your ruling Mr. Speaker.
I rule that the hon. member has completed his statement of privilege, and I must call him to order.
Well, Mr. Speaker-
I have called the hon. member to order.
Is it your ruling, Mr. Speaker, that I cannot proceed?
That is what it means.

Then I appeal from
your ruling, Mr. Speaker.

The hon. member for
South Perth (Mr. Sanderson) having risen to state a question of privilege and having made his statement the Speaker ruled that further remarks on the question were out of order. The hon. member appealed from the Speaker's decision.
I crave the indulgence of the house, Mr. Speaker. I have not made my statement.

In my opinion the statement was complete. The hon, member had neither affirmed nor denied whether he laughed or did not laugh, not that it was a question
of privilege whether he did or did not laugh. I ruled that the question was finished and that there was no necessity of any further remarks, and I called the hon. member to order. He has seen fit to appeal from that decision.
I was paired with the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough (Mr. Embury). Had I voted I would have voted against the ruling.

The house resumed from Friday, June 26, consideration of the motion of the Right Hon. Mr. Bennett for the second reading of Bill No. 47, to provide for the appointment of a tariff board, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Ilsley.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
It is evident that all parties in the house are more or less in agreement as to the advisability of there being some board in the nature of an investigating, fact finding body to assist the government of the day with respect to the tariff and matters incidental thereto. If the bill now before the house did not go further than to make provision for the appointment of an advisory board on tariff and taxation in the nature of a fact finding board there would be no occasion for the amendment which has been moved to the motion for second reading. However, the bill now before the house goes far beyond merely constituting an advisory board on tariff matters, and for that reason it does not meet with the approval of at least the official opposition and I believe, once its provisions are carefully considered, it will not meet with the approval of many other hon. members of this house.
The fact that the present bill goes much beyond what existed heretofore in the nature of an advisory board on tariff matters is evident from the fact that my right hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) was not content to allow the board, which he found in existence on coming into office himself, to remain in office but thought it necessary to dispense entirely with the services of that body and to make provision for another body which would have more extensive powers and some wholly different powers.
The reason given by my right hon. friend for the abolition of the previous board does not seem to me to be a satisfactory one. He said that the old tariff board had not statutory authority. I cannot agree with him in that. The supply bill is a statute, just as is every other bill once it passes both houses and receives royal assent, and express provision was made in the supply bill of 1926 for the

appointment of a tariff board; and in the succeeding years express provision was made in the supply bills for the continuance of the work of that board. The reason given by my right hon. friend is therefore not in itself sufficient to account for the abolition of that board. I believe a reason uppermost in the mind of my right hon. friend was that he had not confidence in the board which he found in office, and to my way of thinking that constituted a sufficient reason for his desiring to change its personnel. However, I do not think it was a sufficient reason summarily to dispense with the entire staff and the general machinery which had been provided. Had my right hon. friend desired to have a board for the purpose of assisting the government in obtaining information on tariff matters, what had been brought into existence under .previous legislation would have been of great assistance to him. If what he had in mind was simply a means of gathering information, there was even less reason for his making a summary change when it is considered that there was a vacancy in the position of chairman of the board. He had the way open to appoint as chairman of the board someone who would be entirely acceptable to himself. So far as the other two members were concerned, I do not suppose that any hon. member on this side of t'he house would have taken more than passing exception to his making a change in the personnel in that particular, if he felt that such action was necessary in order to give him the confidence which he desired to have in a board which was to advise him on tariff matters.
Accordingly, it is necessary to look elsewhere for the real reason. As I said before, one reason was that my right hon. friend had not confidence in the existing board, but he had a further and, I believe, perhaps a more imperative reason. He wished to make wholesale drastic changes in the tariff, and he desired to make those changes without reference to any advisory board. He was about to call a special session of parliament, and although the public did not know it, he knew that he intended at that session to bring in far-reaching changes in the tariff, all of which were to be in an upward direction, so much in an upward direction, many of them, as to be prohibitive. He felt that were any tariff board in existence, whether it was the old board or a board altered in accordance with his own desire to gain more in the way of confidence, it would have been a natural thing for this house to have suggested a reference of the proposed changes to that board before they were made. But, as I said before, my right hon. friend wished to make the
JUNE 29, 1931	[DOT]
Tariff Board*-Mr. Mackenzie King
changes without any such possibility, and so he got rid of the board immediately. May I point out also that at this session he is continuing those drastic, wholesale, upward revisions of the tariff, and is doing so before any new board can come into existence. My right hon. friend made it doubly clear that what he wanted in a tariff board was not a board to advise him as to how to alter the tariff or as to the possible consequences of the alterations he might make, but a board which would work his will with respect to certain other features of the tariff once he had altered the tariff in the way in which he himself proposed. That, I think, is perfectly clear.
I feel more assured in making this statement because of the length of time taken by my right hon, friend on the second reading of this bill to quote from one of the reports of the tariff board in the United States, which, by the way, in many of its particulars, is the board which he is seeking to copy. I have had occasion before to remark how frequently my right hon. friend goes to the United States, not for the best examples of the legislation of that country but for some of the worst features of its legislation. This is another example. He tells the house that this is a board modelled after the tariff board in the United States. It is in some features, some to which we object, although when the provisions of the present bill are read1 it will be seen at once that the sections of the American act which were obviously for the purpose of making the United States board as impartial as possible have not been repeated, and are not to be found1 in this legislation. In referring to the American legislation my right hon. friend quoted at length from a report of the United States board which deals with the tariff on maple sugar, a tariff which the board had found to be too high and had recommended should be reduced. In making the present increases in the tariff no doubt my right hon. friend has had io mind that he will make them of such a character, as to height as well as to extent, that whatever board he appoints will for the balance of the time he is in office-at any rate for this parliament- find its time taken up with lowering duties. These reductions will not be made to an extent to be felt by the consumer to his advantage, 'but will simply be the reduction to lower levels still prohibitive of what at the present time amounts in the case of many changes to a completely prohibitive tariff. It is easy to see that if duties are put at say 100 per cent, and 40 per cent is sufficient to keep out a particular article, the board may well spend days and weeks and months in taking evidence and finally reporting that the 22110-1991
duty should be reduced from 100 to 40 per cent, and still not give any relief to consumers. I believe that once this board is brought into existence that is what it will find itself doing in connection with most of the tariff items which will come before it.
The tariff itself is being widely and materially altered at the present time without reference whatever to any board. That is a rather significant fact, because if the purpose of this board were primarily that of advising the government with regard to tariff changes, then if that purpose has any merit whatever, the proposed changes should certainly be submitted in the first instance to the board so that the government might have the benefit of its advice as to what the effect of the proposed changes will be. That the advisory feature with respect to changes that are likely to affect industry and the well-being of consumers is wholly secondary in the mind of my right hon. friend is evident from the tariff changes he has already introduced, and from the fact that this bill is being introduced only after the tariff has been so drastically and considerably changed. This particular circumstance makes quite clear, wherein the proposed bill in its intent goes far beyond the provisions of any legislation previously existing. The old tariff board was one appointed to consider and advise in advance, upon the effect of any intended changes in the tariff. It was one to which the government of the day submitted its proposed changes.
The extent to which the legislation at present before the house goes beyond making provision for a board which will be purely and simply advisory with regard to tariff changes, is apparent from the provisions of the bill. I shall run over those provisions so as to indicate to hon. members something of the extent of the change. May I also in passing make mention of this fact, that my right hon. friend would probably have left the machinery of the old tariff board in existence as it was until this particular bill was passed had he not felt that with the old machinery still in existence, the contrast between what was there provided and what is provided in the bill which he has introduced would be more marked than it otherwise could be.
Considering then whether or not this measure does not go very much beyond what is needed to provide a fact finding board that is purely advisory, the first section to which I would direct attention is section 3, subsection (3), which reads:
Each member shall hold office during good behaviour for a period of ten years from the date of his appointment, but may be removed for cause at any time by the governor in, council.

Tariff Board-Mr. Mackenzie King
In order to get a board to function as a board of investigation, it is not necessary to make the tenure of office of its members ten years. Indeed, I think my right hon. friend himself, once this measure is passed, if it is passed in this form, will regret the fact once appointments are made that he made them for a period of ten years without affording to his administration any preliminary trial whatever of the adequacy or efficiency of the personnel of the board. He is making it impossible for himself to make a change without adopting a course which will immediately create offence in the mind of someone. That it is not necessary to fix a period of ten years is clear from the fact that the previous administration found no difficulty in securing well qualified members -for a board of investigation without fixing any derm of years at all, and in having all appointments made at pleasure. If that were possible under one administration, it is equally possible under another. I think one has only to consider the nature of the investigation of tariff matters to realize that throughout this country there are many well trained economists and others possessing qualifications necessary to enable them to perform admirably all the duties of an investigating, fact finding board, who would be very glad of an opportunity of serving the government of the country without guarantee other than that their appointments would be at pleasure, or in other words, that the appointment would continue as long as their services were acceptable to the government of the day.
The ten year period is of itself convincing as to the purpose that my right hon. friend has in mind, namely the creation of a body that will be of assistance to the government in matters other than those solely of investigation. Indeed, if one reads subsection (6) of the same section, one will discover that the government has recognized the possibility of obtaining a well qualified person to act even in a temporary capacity. Sob-section (6) of section 3 reads:
If any member by reason of illness or other incapacity is unable at any time to perform the duties of his position, the governor in council may make a temporary appointment of a qualified person to act in his place upon such terms and conditions and for such time as the governor in council may prescribe.
If a qualified person can be found for a temporary post, surely a qualified person can be found for a post which will admit of his being employed during the pleasure of the administration. I need not dwell longer on that, but I shall refer a little later on to the added significance which is given to the ap-

pointment for ten years in virtue of other duties which my right hon. friend is giving to the board.
Section 4, subsection 1, paragraph (b) sets out one of the duties of the board to be appointed. The duty there assigned is entirely new as was pointed out by the hon. member for Hants-Kings (Mr. Ilsley) in his admirable address to the house on moving the amendment which is now before us. Section 4, subsection 1, paragraph (b) reads as follows:
In respect of goods produced in or imported into Canada the board shall, under the direction of the minister, make inquiry as to
(b) the cost of production in Canada and elsewhere, and what increases or decreases in rates of duty are required to equalize differences in the cost of production.
I ask the house to take particular note of these words: "What increases or decreases in rates of duty are required." That goes very much further than simply finding facts. I am sure every hon. member will see that at least it means the drawing of inferences. As the hon. member who has moved the amendment has said, it goes the length of helping to form opinions. I should be inclined to believe it goes the length of duty-making, of actually determining what the duty shall be for a particular purpose, of advising and giving the ministry the grounds for its policy and its action alike, in fixing particular rates of duty. At page 3083 of Hansard my right hon. friend, in speaking of the board's function in this particular, is reported as having said:	" It has to determine what duty is
necessary." May I say to my right hon. friend, when he introduced the resolution upon which this bill was based, he told us specifically that this board would not have the right to draw any inferences. That there may be no doubt about the matter, may I quote for my right hon. friend the page of unrevised Hansard in which he states that the board will not have the right to draw any inferences.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: There is no doubt about that.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
I refer to page 1782 of Hansard. As my right hon. friend admits this, I need not read what he said, his words were: "inferences are not to be drawn by the board." If the board is not to have the right of drawing inferences, how is it going to be able to determine what increases or decreases in rates of duty are required in order to equalize differences in costs of production? That is all clearly in the nature of inference, as a result of investiga-

Tariff Board-Mr. Mackenzie King
ti-on. It is drawing inferences. It is helping in that way to determine actually what increases of duty will be imposed.
There is another subsection of the same section which makes it also apparent that not only with respect to the rates of duty but also with respect to prices this board will be expected to perform an important function, a function which comes well-nigh determining at what particular prices commodities are to be kept fixed, nominally to save the consumer from exploitation, but in reality in many cases undoubtedly to keep prices at a particular level. Paragraphs (e) and (f) of section 4 read as follows, referring to matters to be inquired into by the board:.
(e)	all conditions and factors which affect or enter into the cost of production and the price to the consumers in Canada;
(f)	generally, all the conditions affecting production, manufacture, cost and price in Canada as compared with other countries.
In other words, this board will be expected to inquire into the matter of prices at which certain commodities are being sold in Canada in comparison with the prices in other countries, and both in relation to the cost of production; and the government of the day in virtue of the legislation which it is introducing will unquestionably base its tariff action upon the inferences drawn in that regard. The board's conclusions will become the determining factor in regulating prices as well as rates of duties, on the pretext of saving the consumer from exploitation, in reality to protect this manufacturer in the sale of his commodities within the country as well as against competition from without.
As was pointed out by the hon. member for Hants-Kings (Mr. Ilsley) in quoting Professor [DOT] Taussig of Harvard, who had had three or four years' experience as a member of the tariff board in the United States, it is an impossibility for any board to attempt to determine what increases or decreases in rates of duty are required in order to equalize differences in the cost of production, or what is necessary with respect to the cost and prices of commodities, and to that end to make comparisons between prices and costs in different countries. One has but to ask oneself what are the difficulties in one's own country of determining what goes to make up the costs of production of any commodity to realize that if the board's functions were limited to that alone it would have just about all it could attempt to do; but hon. members will realize that citizens of another country are not going to permit a board of a foreign nation to examine into their industries, investigate their books, and determine comparative costs. It is perfectly clear that in that regard the function which assumedly is being given to this board is one thait it will find it impossible to perform. Nevertheless, being given that power, the board is to determine what increases or decreases in rates of duty are necessary to make costs of production in this country equal to what they are in other countries. Moreover this task could it be performed and were it acted upon, would put an end to all international trade.
I pass on to the next subsection, which also indicates very clearly wherein the proposed board goes much further than being merely a fact finding body to advise the government with respect to tariffs as a result of investigation. Subsection 2 of section 4 reads as follows:
The board shall make inquiry into any other matter, upon which the minister desires information, in relation to any goods which, if brought into Canada or produced in Canada, are subject to or exempt from duties of customs or excise, and shall report to the minister, and the inquiry into any such matter may include inquiry as to the effect which an increase or decrease of the existing rate of duty upon a given commodity might have upon industry or trade, and the extent to which the consumer is protected from exploitation.
I ask hon. members to note those words, "the effect which an increase or decrease of the existing rate of duty upon a given commodity might have upon industry or trade, and the extent to which the consumer is protected from exploitation." When a board is asked to report upon the effect of anything, it is not merely reporting on the facts; it is drawing conclusions. In fact, an inquiry of that kind would require the board itself to make an investigation into the effects of the existing tariffs, and so far as its members had any preconceived views regarding the virtue of tariffs or the reverse, their judgment in a matter of that kind would certainly be biased and be affected by their views.
I pass on to the next subsection:
The board may be empowered by the governor in council to hold an inquiry under section fifteen of the Customs Tariff, in the same manner as the judge of the exchequer court or any other judge therein referred to may be so empowered, and the said section shall include and apply to the board as if it were therein expressly named.
Here is a very wide departure. This goes completely beyond any power given at any previous time to a board of investigation. This subsection will empower the board to exercise functions which to-day can only be exercised under section 15 of the Custom* Tariff. Section 15 of the Customs Tariff was inserted in order to give to the consumers of the country the benefit of a judicial inquiry
3142	COMMONS
Tariff Board-Mr. Mackenzie King
conducted by members of the judiciary, who are entirely removed from politics, who in no way owe their appointment to the views they may hold on fiscal questions, and who are entirely removed from any government influence or control. They are given the power of making an investigation where it is thought that the customs tariff is operating in a way that is detrimental to consumers or producers. Once this particular subsection is on the statute book the government will be able to turn over to a board of its own appointees the duty of making an investigation which at the present time can only be made by a judge of the exchequer court or some other judge to whom the matter may be referred. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that we should be very careful before we take away from the people of this country this slight degree of judicial protection which they now have with respect to the effects of a customs tariff and allow the government of the day instead to refer the subject matter of investigation to a board of its own creation, a board which cannot be other than biased, a board the appointees of which share the views of the government with respect to the tariff. The judiciary is an independent body. No matter could come before any of its members unless it were so serious as to be brought under section IS of the Customs Tariff. But once the present measure is passed the functions of the judiciary will for this purpose to all intents and purposes be usurped by a body, which, as I have said, has been appointed by the ministry of the day to further its own particular views with regard to what the tariff policy of this country should be. That is a very serious alteration to permit.
May I point out further that by this change the government is making of the proposed tariff board not a board of investigation, but a court. There is no question about that being, the principal intention. My right hon. friend did not lead the house to believe when he was introducing his measure that what he intended to do was to add to the number of the courts in the country, but he did tell us on the second reading of the bill that what he was establishing as a new court.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: I said that on the resolution-a court of record.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
Possibly my
right hon. friend did, and I beg his pardon if I have overlooked that fact. The point I wish to bring out is this. He did not stress what I believe to be the essential feature of this bill, that it is creating a new court to deal with tariff matters; matters far beyond any mere question of investigation for pur-

poses of -mere fact-finding. The establishment of a new court to deal with tariff matters as though they were matters of property and civil rights is the primary purpose of this bill; I do not think that my right hon. friend will deny that, and to that extent it goes far beyond anything which this parliament has previously countenanced as a part of the function of an advisory board intended only to advise on tariff matters. I do not wish to .say that the members whom my right hon. friend will appoint to the board will be intentionally partisan. That would be going too far, and we cannot say, until we see how they perform their duties to what extent their partisanship may extend. The public in general however will at least have the feeling that such protection as is afforded them to-day by the courts under the section of the Customs Tariff to which I have referred will be taken away or of no avail and that hereafter they will be at .the mercy of a board of partisans appointed by the administration of the day.
May I refer to the next suDsection, which is subsection 4 of section 4 of the bill. It reads as follows:
The governor in council may empower the board to make any investigation or hold any inquiry authorized by the provisions of the Combines Investigation Act, or of a relative nature, and for these purposes the board shall have all the powers, authority and jurisdiction vested in the registrar or in a commissioner appointed under that act to hold investigations.
I ask the house to consider for a moment or two the purposes of the Combines Investigation Act. It was passed to enable consumers or producers who believed their interests were being adversely affected by tariffs, through combinations or monopolies in restraint of trade formed as a result of tariffs or in other ways, to have the protection of an investigation conducted in a manner in which they would have reason to feel a degree of confidence. The old Combines Investigation Act which was introduced and passed in this house in the year 1910 provided that parties who felt they were being adversely affected by a monopoly, trust, merger or the like might apply for inquiry by a board of investigation and in the event of a prima facie case being made out might themselves name a member of the board of investigation. In turn the trust, monopoly or whatever concern was charged with operating against the interests of the public was permitted to name a member of the board. If the two parties interested could agree upon a chairman they were permitted so to do, and in the event of their not agreeing the government of the day was empowered to appoint a chairman. Before

Tariff Board-Mr. Mackenzie King
the body thus approved the parties interested were entitled to have their own representatives appear and they were likely as a consequence to have confidence in such a body. The old board provided a great protection to parties in this country against monopolies and mergers operating to the detriment of the public behind the shelter of a protective tariff. That act remained on the statutes from the year 1910 until the year 1919 when the then government of the day, a Conservative administration, repealed the act and substituted therefor a board of commerce. The board of commerce was to have to do with the administration of a Fair Prices Act, as it was termed and enacted at that time. I do not think at this time I need go into the history of the board of commerce and the Fair Prices Act. Hon. members will recall that the board of commerce was in the nature of a court. Hon. members may also recall that one of the judges resigned because he felt the operations of that board were biased in favour of special interests and not in accordance with the best interests of the people. The legality of the legislation was very shortly after its enactment called in question, an appeal was made to the supreme court and was carried subsequently to the privy council. The judicial committee of the privy council declared the legislation to be ultra vires.

Because the statute was enacted in peace times; it was repealed in peace times; and I hope we are still in peace times.
At any rate when the legislation was declared ultra vires it was repealed. I submit that an examination of the legislation now before us will convince any hon. member that the government is seeking, under the guise of a court differently named, to restore something resembling the old board of commerce. The duties assigned to the board under this bill are very similar to those the board of commerce had when it was called to administer the Fair Prices Act. The court that is now being formed, among other duties, is to have the obligation-if the government chooses to assign it the obligation-of administering an all important part of the Combines Investigation Act.
When the Board of Commerce Act and the Fair Prices Act were repealed, a new enactment was brought foiward by the Liberal administration of the day in 1923. Another Combines Investigation Act, framed in the way the government of the day believed would best secure the confidence of those on whose behalf it was enacted, was placed again upon the statutes. To all intents and purposes the legislation now before us has for its puipose the abolition of the real intent of that combines legislation because if the government so desires all the duties prescribed under the statute creating the Combines Investigation Act, as reenacted in 1923, may be withheld from the parties entrusted with inquiry imder the Combines Investigation Act and passed over to the new board, which as I have already said, is a body chosen to further the government's point of view on tariff matters. To my mind such a possible change is of a most serious nature. May I make mention of the further fact, that the validity of the Combines Investigation Act of 1923 has been tested in the courts. Certain interests which believed the act was operating in a manner which made it difficult for them to carry on their alleged combine or monopoly, brought an action to test the validity of the act. The Supreme Court of Canada upheld the validity of the act and the case was carried to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. The judicial committee upheld the decision of the supreme court.
With regard to the legislation before us, we are therefore in the curious position that provision is being made whereby for legislation which has stood the test of the highest courts in Canada and the empire there may be substituted by the government a procedure wholly similar to that of the Board of Commerce in its administration of the Fair Prices Act, which was declared by the courts to be ultra vires. To point out clearly the parallel between the two cases may I state that by the Board of Commerce Act a board was set up consisting of three commissioners appointed by the governor in council and given the powers of a court of record. The duty of the board was to administer the second of the two statutes in question, namely the Combines and Fair Prices Act, called the Special Act. The present bill constitutes the tariff board a court of record. It is to make inquiries into the prices received by producers, manufacturers, wholesalers, dealers, retailers and other distributors, and note all conditions and factors which affect or enter into the prices to consumers in Canada. As in the case with respect to the protection given consumers and

Tariff Board-Mr. Mackenzie King
producers by the provisions of the Customs Act relating to judicial inquiry in certain cases my right bon. friend is again giving to the governor in council the power to take away from the consumers and producers of Canada the remedy which at the present time under the Combines Investigation Act they enjoy, of having investigation made by persons appointed under an act framed especially to win their confidence, and afford them protection; and is placing them at the mercy of a board which I think I may safely say will be of his own particular bent of mind in conducting an investigation.
I know my right hon. friend will say he is not repealing the Combines Investigation Act. Certainly he is not repealing it, but by giving to the governor in council power to have investigations made by this special court rather than before the parties named in the Combines Investigation Act, and there empowered to investigate a combine, or before a judge as set out in the section of the Customs Tariff to which I have referred, he is doing something much more subtle and far reaching.
May I at this point give a concrete illustration. We will assume for the moment that the consumers of gasoline in this country entertain the view that the prices of gasoline are too high and that by virtue of protection which has been given by the present administration a combine or monopoly has come into existence which is operating to their detriment. At the present time under section 15 of the Customs Tariff an investigation may be held before a judge of the Exchequer Court or of some other court, or an investigation may be held under the provisions of the Combines Investigation Act. There are the two existing alternatives. My right hon. friend, under the legislation which he is now seeking to enact, could, were it passed, say, ''We will not permit an inquiry to take place before a member of the judiciary or under the provisions of the Combines Investigation Act, we will refer it to this board which we have created, and its decision will govern in the matter." I do not think I need go further in illustrating the danger underlying the proposed legislation as to the extent to which consumers and producers may find themselves, once it is enacted, without some of the security and protection afforded in existing legislation.
I come now to subsection 5 of section 5:
The board shall have the same power to enforce the attendance of witnesses, and to compel them to give evidence, as is vested in any court of record in civil cases.

And subsection 6:
The board shall be a court of record, and have an official seal which shall be judicially noticed.
There can no longer be any mistake about what my right hon. friend has in mind: iit is the creation of a court; a court of very wide powers and authority, a new and very important court. In fact on the second reading of this bill my right hon. friend termed it a "federal court"; he spoke of those who would be members of it as judges; and on the resolution he said, "the board will be in every sense a judicial tribunal." Apart altogether from any such tribunal being necessary for mere purposes of investigation and fact-finding, I question very much the wisdom of trying to deal with social and economic problems by the establishment of courts of law or of attempting to find their solution along lines of procedure such as are adopted in the courts. There is a difference between what I might call legal phenomena- phenomena that has largely to do with questions of property, civil rights and the like, and economic phenomena which affect the wellbeing of individuals in their homes and in their several occupations. Matters of wages, of prices, ithe cost of living, and the like-all economic phenomena-are not of a character which can be determined satisfactorily in a court of law. Whether the economic problems to be solved relate to the tariff or to anything else affecting social conditions, a different method of investigation is desirable if the interests and well-being of the people are to be the primary consideration.
May I say that parliament has already carefully noted that fact. This is not the first Statute considered by this house which has to do with the investigation of economic phenomena, and the attempted solution of the problems to which they relate. There are already on the statutes several enactments framed with a view to aiding in the solution of social and economic problems. One of these statutes I might mention-the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, which was passed in 1907. That act, as hon. members know, has been amended on one or two occasions, but in its essentials it remains pretty much to-day what it was when it was enacted twenty-five years ago. The outstanding feature of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act is that it provides for the creation of boards for the investigation of industrial disputes, but care is taken that the appointees to these boards are persons in whom the parties themselves have confidence. For example, the workingmen on their part are permitted to name a

Tarifj Board-Mr. Mackenzie King
member, the employers on their part are also permitted to name a member, they being the two parties primarily affected, and if those two members can agree upon the third member they nominate him; if not, the government does so. The board thus formed has all the powers of a court; it may summon witnesses, take evidence, compel the production of documents and the like. These powers are available if the necessity for their exercise arises. But what for a quarter of a century has been the experience of the operation of boards appointed under that legislation? The experience has been that those strictly legal features are seldom availed of, and that when availed of they are of very questionable value; that the real value of such boards from the point of view of investigation is that the parties concerned are able to meet together in the presence of each other, and in the presence of the public, and there bring out the essential facts which govern the question under investigation -for example, exact statements as to wages, hours and other conditions of employment prevailing in the industry affected here and elsewhere. The three parties meet together- the representatives of the employers, the employees and the government respectively- and endeavour by question and answer ;md examination of documents, premises and the like to get at the facts. If there is a dispute between the parties themselves as to one not telling the truth, then resort is had to the legal machinery for securing evidence under oath. But in practice that necessity has very seldom arisen. Boards of investigation have found it possible to get the fullest information by informal consideration of the questions in dispute.
Now, my right hon. friend has taken some 'exception to what he speaks of as the informal manner in which information pertaining to the tariff has been obtained. I cannot agree with him that if the object is primarily that of ascertaining the facts that object will not be furthered much more effectively by bringing into one room in the presence of others those who are primarily concerned, and have them then and there admit or deny what is essential in the investigation. Take, for example, an investigation into tariff matters affecting any particular industry. If those engaged in the industry and consumers who are affected by the prices of the products of the industry are all permitted to meet together in a common discussion, and all agree upon a statement of the facts, or if need be give testimony where controversy arises, what better method can there possibly be of eliciting the
truth in regard to any situation? That was the method under which the former board proceeded. Where there is an issue between the parties as to who is telling the truth, it may become necessary to resort to legal procedure. But I do submit that if the object be that of fact finding and getting at the truth of the situation, the less there is of putting men under oath and going through the formalities of court procedure, particularly in the case of persons who for the most part abhor the thought of being brought into court for any purpose, the better in the end it will be for the purposes an investigation is intended to serve.
One of the most successful chairman of boards of investigation and conciliation under the industrial disputes act was the late Professor Adam Shortt. As hon. members well know, he was chairman of a very large number of such boards. In nearly all cases Professor Shortt was able to ascertain the facts without resort to legal methods and by presenting the truth of the situation to the parties concerned to have them accept the findings that became obvious in the light of the truth. That was a great tribute not only to the professor, but an equally great tribute to human nature itself, in that it discloses that men when they recognize the truth are prepared to accept it; if parties having different interests, after being brought together, can come to agree on the facts, there ceases to be any longer much that requires settlement between them.
A day or two ago I read in the journal of the Canadian Bankers' Association of April, of this year, a brief editorial on Professor Shortt, which was published shortly after his death. I came across this paragraph, which is so pertinent that I ask permission to read it:
He was chairman of all the more important boards appointed during the first few years of the act. Here he made a distinctive contribution which was vital to the effective working of the legislation. He saw that if success was to be achieved the investigations of the board set up must work toward conciliation and not attempt to act as a court of arbitration. Still more, legal technicalities must not be allowed to interfere with the main business of arriving at an agreement. With this principle firmly grasped he successfully eliminated formal court procedure and attained remarkable success in a number of amicable agreements which were reached. The later history of the act proved abundantly his wisdom. It became later the custom to appoint judges and lawyers as presiding officers of boards and from that day the effectiveness of the legislation waned, and finally legal procedure entirely obliterated the legislation when the privy council held the act ultra vires in 1925.

I submit, Mr. Speaker, that with respect to the economic phenomena of which account must be taken in dealing with tariff matters, there is no essential difference from that with respect to which account must be taken in dealing with questions of wages or prices in industrial disputes or as regards restrictions upon trade, because they are all inter-related; in fact it is in relation to questions of wages and prices and the like that the whole tariff discussion and controversy arises. I do submit that unless there is some motive beyond that of seeking to get at the facts, so that the government may be fully apprised of them in taking any steps in regard to the tariff, it would be much better to eliminate the court feature altogether and hold to a method of inquiry, which, up to the present, has proved so successful in different as well as allied fields. But the fact that my right hon. friend is creating a court to which he has given such powers makes convincingly clear, to my mind, an ulterior object other than that of mere investigation. What this objective is I shall endeavour to show in a few moments.
My right hon. friend is creating not a simple court with moderate powers; not an ordinary court like a county court; he is establishing one of the largest and most powerful courts in the country. He himself has termed it a federal court; it is a federal court with very large powers and very large remuneration so far as its members are concerned. Powers such as are given to this court are not needed at all for purposes of investigation in tariff matters. The bill makes no provision for the immediate publication of all the proceedings of the court, it does contain however provision for part of the work being carried on in secret. The bill gives to the court power to compel the taking of evidence under oath, if it so desires, but on the other hand it contains a provision which enables the members of the court to act on information which they obtain anywhere and in any way. I ask my right hon. friend:	What is the sense of including in
the bill a provision which enables the court to take evidence under oath if, at the same time, we are going to give to the members of the court the right to make equal use of information which they obtain in any way, at any time? In order that there may be no mistake about it let me read subsection (5) of section 5 of the act:
(5) The board shall have the same power to enforce the attendance of witnesses, and to compel them to give evidence, as is vested in any court of record in civil cases.

Then subsection (9) of the same section reads:
/9) For the purpose of any inquiry under this act, the board may obtain information, which in their judgment is authentic, otherwise than under the sanction of an oath or affirmation, and use apd act upon such information.
My right hon. friend is not only creating a court; he is creating a star chamber court. He is giving to this body the power to put a man on his oath, when it suits its members so to do. On the other hand they may gather information not in the nature of evidence on oath and act upon it if it suits them so to do. They can meet in secret if they desire so to do, and can prevent the publication of any of the evidence which they do not wish published. More than that, the bill goes the length of containing a provision which permits the arrest and imprisonment of individuals who happen to be present when the board may be discussing certain matters, or when certain matters are being discussed before the board if, perchance, at any time those individuals disclose some of the information which the board thinks it is in the public interest not to have disclosed. I ask whether you could have a court which is more in the nature of a star chamber court than one which carries on some of its proceedings in secret; one that can act on whatever information it pleases; one that need not, unless it so desires, report its proceedings, except in the form of a prepared report, and one which has given to it as well arbitrary powers of fine and imprisonment. Surely in matters of tariff, which affect simply the economic life of the people, we have not reached the point in 'Canada where we have to create boards in the nature of criminal courts in order to get information which will assist the government. I must say frankly to my hon. friend that after reading this legislation, one begins to wonder what, in his view, government is for; whether to his mind government is here to serve the interests of the people or whether it is here to create special courts for certain special interests, courts which will enable those interests to gain a control over an economic situation which is denied the rest of the people, and which could not be secured by them in any other way.
The other evening I spoke about where this whole legislation with respect to tariff matters is tending. I said my right hon. friend was creating an industrial feudalism in this country, I gave to the house certain of the incidents of feudalism of which I thought it would not be difficult to discover

Tariff Board-Mr. Mackenzie King
the counterparts in the industrial world of today as it will more and more become if legislation of this kind goes through. One of the incidents of feudalism to which I then referred was the right claimed by the lords of the day not to be subject to the ordinary courts, but to have their own special courts in which matters affecting themselves and their special interests would be tried. Here we have a special court being created for special interests who are coming to this parliament for special favours, and we are giving to those who are seeking protection in this fashion the right to have their own court and to have all the protection a court of that kind throws around them. I say, Mr. Speaker, that my right hon. friend is going pretty far in denying what are the fundamental rights of the people of the country when he goes the length in the special protection of specially favoured interests he does in this legislation.
Now may I refer to one or two other sections. Just in passing I draw attention to section 7 of subsection 5:
There shall be employed in the service of the board such officers, clerks and other employees as the governor in council may see fit to appoint, and they shall respectively receive such salaries or remuneration as may be approved by the governor in council.
Not only is my right hon. friend appointing the judges; he is also appointing the officers, clerks and other employees of this particular board or count. He is not allowing the Civil Service Commission to make the appointments; he is not allowing, as was the practice under the other board, the appointments to be made by the board itself. He is making all appointments himself, and just here may I say to my right hon. friend that when he was speaking on the resolution he gave this house to understand directly the opposite. He told the house that these officers, clerks and employees *would be appointed by the board; he did not say they would be appointed by himself. Now when the bill comes before the house we'see that it contains a provision that they shall be appointed by the governor in council instead of by the board. I hope my right hon. friend will give further consideration to this matter when we are discussing the section.

In that case the board itself recommended who the appointees were to be, it was not the governor in council that made the selections. The bill is providing not that the board shall make the appointments but that the governor in council shall appoint everyone who has anything to do with the board which is being called into existence.
May I again point out that my remarks all along the way have been directed to these provisions as exemplifying the intention of the government to go much farther in this legislation than simply to appoint a board to investigate for the purpose of assisting the government in the formulation of tariffs or matters incidental thereto.
There is another section of the bill which will make clear to hon. members whether there is the necessity of going the length to which this legislation goes, if investigating and getting at the facts is all that my right hon. friend has in mind. Section 8 subsection (1) reads as follows:
Every member who has served on the board for a period of at least ten years may be granted an annuity for the term of his natural life equal to one-fourth of the annual salary received by him during such period, and if he lias served for any period less than ten years but more than five years, he may be granted an annuity equal to one-fifth of the annual salary received by him during such period.
Subsection (2) reads:
The chairman of the board shall be paid an annual salary of twelve thousand dollars, and the other two members shall each be paid an annual salary of ten thousand dollars.
Let us consider these salaries for a moment. The members of this board, which is to be simply a farct finding body, are to receive $12,000 and $10,000 annually. The chairman is to receive $12,000 per year for a ten year appointment, and in addition to that, at the end of the ten years he is to receive an annuity of $3,000. The other members are each to receive $10,000 per year, and an

May I point out to the house that ministers of the crown receive nothing in the way of an annuity. If it is possible to find hon. gentlemen who are prepared to accept the position of a minister of the crown for $10,000 per year, without any annuity, to take an office, precarious as it is, and with all that it involves in the way of work from morn to eve and long after, I fail to see why it should be necessary to pay these very large salaries to the members of this board unless something of a quite exceptional character is going to be expected of them. There is nothing in investigating and factfinding with respect to prices, wages, costs and the like which merits the payment of these salaries. The type of man best qualified to carry on the work of investigation is the trained economist. I think the house will agree with me that men of the type of the late Dr. Adam Shortt, men who hold distinguished positions as professors of political economy in our universities, or men specially ' trained in other Spheres, are of the type best qualified for positions of the kind. I am quite sure that the services of men of this type could be obtained by the state at salaries similar in amount to those paid by the universities. My right hon. friend is going pretty far in establishing a board which rivals the supreme court as far as salaries of its members and some of its powers are concerned. I believe it goes farther than the Board of Railway Commissioners and the Civil Sendee Commission. I should say that my right hon. friend has gone quite the limit.
I come now to the next portion of the act, which makes it abundantly clear that the purpose of this legislation is to appoint a board for other than fact finding purposes. Part II of the bill entitled "Tariff Board substituted for Board of Customs," and section 11 reads as follows:

(1)	From and after a date to be fixed by the governor in council, all the powers, functions and duties of the board of customs shall be assigned to and be transacted by the tariff board constituted by this act.
(2)	Wherever in any act of the parliament of Canada, or in any regulations, or orders made thereunder, the board of customs is mentioned or referred to, the tariff board shall in each and every case be substituted therefor.
Subsection (4) reads as follows:
(4) The board shall have such powers and perform such duties under this part as are assigned to it by any act of the parliament of Canada or by the governor in council.
While that section may serve a very useful purpose, I can see where it may also serve a very dangerous one. I take it that my right hon. friend is establishing a board which will be in accord with his own views on tariff matters. He proposes to make that board a court which will have the last word in respect to the interpretation of statutes and orders in council, and in respect to matters of administration of the customs of this country. As matters now stand, there is at least an appeal from the board of customs to the governor in council, but in his legislation my right hon. friend does not provide for any such appeal. It is true that on the second reading he said that he was open-minded as to whether or not there should be an appeal to the governor in council, but he has made no provision therefor. I hope he will leave at least that much to his possible successors. I do not suppose it makes much difference while he himself is in office, but in respect to these matters I do not think that there should be any board which would have the last and final word with respect to the interpretation to be placed on the legislation of this parliament with respect to tariff and other revenue matters or any orders in council passed by the government under authority of this parliament with respect to the same. I would again direct the attention of the house to subsection 4, which reads:
The board shall have such powers and perform such duties under this part as are assigned to it by any act of the parliament of Canada or by the governor in council.
That subsection gives the governor in council the power to assign to the board special duties, and permits the board to go ahead and interpret tariff legislation under those special duties. As yet we do not know what powers the governor in council may give this board under this particular subsection. We are being asked to allow a board that is going to have the final say in matters of administration of the tariff, to be permitted to do so in the light of any powers which may yet be

Tariff Board-Mr. Mackenzie King
given, to it by the governor in council. It is plain that the purpose of this legislation is quite other than that of appointing a board merely to investigate and advise concerning tariff matters.
There are other grounds from which I draw this inference. One of them is found in the explanatory note in the bill.

There must be in his mind something which I have touched upon at the moment. The explanatory notes read:
The purpose of this bill is to create a tariff board.
First of all, my right hon. friend will notice that the word "advisory" is omitted. It is a tariff board, not an advisory board on tariff, as was the case with the board he abolished. It is a board which, as he himself has said, is to be in the nature of a court. Then the explanatory note says:
It is not the intention to delegate to the board the duty and responsibility resting upon the government of originating bills for the raising of revenue, which will remain precisely as at present. The intention is to secure, as a result of the work of the board, a constantly increasing body of information which will he of service to the government and parliament.
I ask the house to notice just what is expressed in that explanatory note:
It is not the intention to delegate to the board the duty and responsibility resting upon the government of originating bills for the raising of revenue, which will remain precisely as at present.
The originating of bills for the raising of revenue could not by any conceivable means rest anywhere else than with the government and parliament. Obviously that could not be done by anybody other than the government with the assistance of parliament. But in the interpretation of that paragraph- and -here I hope my right hon. friend will tell me whether or not I am misjudging him -one has to have in mind the view that my right hon. friend entertains with respect to the tariff. He takes the view that the tariff may be a tax; he also takes the view that the tariff may not be a tax. I think I am right in saying that. He has repeatedly made that statement, and his words will be found in Hansard of the last special session. So far as the tariff is being considered as a tax, it will be a matter affecting the revenues, and my right hon. friend says: Now, so far as the revenue is concerned, certainly parliament will continue to deal with that. But what about the functions of this board when the tariff is being viewed, not as something concerned with revenue but as something in the nature of protection to industry apart from revenue altogether? There, I submit, is where we discover the whole purpose and intent of this legislation; it is to form a board in the nature of a court which will maintain the protective feature in all matters pertaining to the tariff. That is the object of it; my right hon. friend knows it, and I do not think he will deny it. It is important that the house should know and understand that the aim of this legislation is to call into being a federal court, give it, as I have said, all the powers of a star chamber, appoint its members for a period of ten years so that their tenure of office will outrun that of one or two parliaments and possibly three, and have them placed there in control over the tariff as it affects prices, wages, cost of production and the like, in order to see that at all times and at all costs the protective principle is retained in the tariff and matters related thereto.
I wish to say just a word on this point to some of the supporters of my right hon. friend on the other side who come from other parts of the dominion than those which it is hoped most to benefit by this legislation. I speak particularly to some of those who come from the maritime provinces, and some who come from the west. I do not ask you to cease to give your support to your leader, but I suggest, in the interests of those whom you represent and your own interests, having regard to the future, you take occasion to point out just what the people of the constituencies from which you come are likely to feel
