subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: But the legislation is introduced with the idea that the board is to see that the protective principle is maintained.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: That arises in the imagination of the right hon. gentleman.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
There is no
question about what I have said. The country will soon agree with me.
Let us consider the remainder of the reference made to the board as a fact finding body. The explanatory note says:
The intention is to secure, as a result of the work of the board, a constantly increasing body of information which will be of service to the government and parliament.
In other words, a sort of by-product of the work of the board is to be the information they collect while they are seeing to it that the protective principle is maintained intact. That is the significance of the legislation which we now have before us.
As I have said, this legislation to be understood aright must be interpreted in the light of the policies of my right hon. friend as he himself has stated them in parliament and throughout the country. In Great Britain

he made it quite clear that the aim of his policy was protection for the industries of this country to the extent of keeping out of Canada commodities or goods which can be produced or manufactured here. He made equally clear in his statement on the budget that one of our first duties was to see that goods did not come in from foreign countries if they could be produced or manufactured in Canada. He will not deny that. All this legislation with respect to creating a court to study costs of production, prices and the like has to do with the objective which my right hon. friend has in mind. So far as he and his administration are concerned, he may with the object he has in view be quite right in doing what he has done. But I come now to the really serious part of the matter, which is that my right hon. friend is seeking to bind not only his own administration but subsequent administrations. He is seeking not only to bind this parliament with respect to this legislation but to inflict its provisions upon subsequent parliaments for at least a number of years to come.
Just at this point may I pause to make clear why it is that some of us feel as strongly as we do and why we believe the country will feel very strongly about legislation of this kind being fastened irrevocably on Canada for a term of years. It may be thought that when my right hon. friend goes to the country in due time, should the issue be one relating to the tariff, and the party opposed to him be returned to power, all they would have to do would be to repeal this legislation and the evil of it would be removed. That is what I have no doubt is generally believed, but may I point out to hon. members and the country that legislation can be repealed only by both houses of parliament and by the assent of the governor general. May I point out further that at the present time the position of political parties in the other house is that both parties are at the moment just about evenly represented. In the course of the next few years the appointments which will be made by my right hon. friend to the Senate will all be appointments from the Conservative party in this country. That means that should another government be returned, even if it desire to do so, and even if the question of repeal be made an issue in the election, it cannot repeal this legislation, because any proposal to effect repeal would require the approval of both houses of parliament. I say that my right hon. friend has no right so to bind subsequent governments or subsequent parliaments. If the legislation were not of the character it is,

Tariff Board-Mr. Mackenzie King
the matter would not be so serious. But since it is legislation aimed at actually shackling the country for years to come with my right hon. friend's particular brand of high protection it becomes a matter for serious consideration whether this [DOT] house should permit legislation to be passed under which a term of ten years is fixed during which members of the board constituted by it shall hold office.
I want to point out to my right hon. friend how absolutely unfair anything of that kind is. All questions relating to the tariff are matters of policy. I am sure that my right hon. friend whatever he may say or do will agree with me that if in matters of tariff policy a government is seeking advice, it is entitled to have as advisers those in whom it has confidence. My right hon. friend will not deny that his government is a protectionist government, and that those who are opposed to him are not high protectionists, that those opposed to him, if they believe in protection, believe in low protection; that for the most part they view the tariff rather from the point of view of revenue than from the protective principle. How then can he justify under circumstances which may arise asking an administration that believes in low tariffs or tariffs for revenue to accept for purposes of adlvice on tariff matters a court that has been created by himself, believing, as he does, in high protection? How can he ask an administration opposed to his own to allow such a court to have a final say with regard to the interpretation of its policies in many details?

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: It has not the final say.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: I have pointed out that it has.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: That is in your imagination.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: My hon. friend is quite mistaken. Will he say that transferring to this new board all the powers that are to-day expressed by the customs board is not giving it a final say similar to that which the customs board has? He knows that it is.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
It is not final so far as
the customs board is concerned, but my right hon. friend was speaking of the tariff board.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
That is what
I am saying. This legislation takes away the right which exists to-day of an appeal from the customs board.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
The governor in council,
as a court of appeal, is non-partisan.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
May I ask my right hon. friend this question: Would he accept as a body of advisers for his term of
office a body appointed by myself and those who sit around me were we in office and I left it to him as a legacy?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: I had to.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
He says that
he had to, but he did not. We left him a tariff board, composed of very able men, a board which had functioned efficiently, and his first act was to abolish that board.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: That was not a nonpartisan board.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
I am not discussing whether it was partisan or not. I submit tha/t any government would be derelict in its duty to its own party if it did not select as its advisers on tariff masters men in whom it had confidence, and whose advice it was prepared to trust. It is so much a matter of common sense that no one can dispute the assertion for a moment. My right hon. friend by his very act in abolishing the tariff board that was in existence when he came into office completely answers the contention he seeks to make that there is any justification for naming a board that will continue in office for a longer period than "at pleasure." He has shown by his own act that he himself believes that "at pleasure" is the only length of time that a board of this character should be permitted to hold office. I put this to my right hon. friend: Assume that you have two parties, one believing strongly in protection, and the other believing in tariff for revenue. Is it fair that a protectionist government should be advised by a tariff-for-revenue board, or that a tariff-for-revenue government should be advised by a high protectionist board? I think the fair and square view which the public is likely to take of this matter will be sufficient to make clear the injustice of the present position which my right hon. friend is taking.
But may I give to my right hon. friend an authority which I hope that he at least will accept, as to the wrong principle which he is seeking to have adopted in this legislation? The present Prime Minister when in opposition gave to the house and the country his views with respect to what in the matter of having one parliament bind another was sound in principle. In his statement the other day my right hon. friend went much farther than simply having one parliament bind another. He says he believes that one government should have the right to bind another. "In my judgment it is essential that the board should hold office beyond the term of office of a government," were his
3152	COMMONS
Tariff Board-Mr. Mackenzie King
exact words. He believes he should enact legislation which will bind subsequent governments. I say that that is going very, very much too far. If he had said, bind subsequent parliaments, he would have been going pretty far; but when he says, bind subsequent governments, he goes altogether too far.
When I was in the position which my right hon. friend is occupying to-day, I brought in a measure to appropriate to the Federal District Commission a sum of money, not a very large sum, for a period of thirty years. The amount was for the purpose of maintaining the park and driveway system of the capital over which the Federal District Commission has control. Every member knows that as long as Ottawa remains the capital there will have to be a sum of money put aside for the maintenance of its parks and drives. All we were asking was that the sum to be put aside should be guaranteed for a number of years, so that there would be no doubt in the mind of anyone as to that work being properly cared for. Speaking on that bill, my right hon. friend laid down the principle which in respect of binding subsequent parliaments he said should govern. Let me read what he said. It is rather a coincidence that he was assisted on that occasion by the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin), who on this same matter helped out on the declaration of principle. I quote from Hansard, page 2352, of the debates of April 24, 1928. Here the present Prime Minister lays down the principle which should govern with respect to binding a subsequent parliament or a subsequent government:
I cannot think it quite consonant with the ideas of the right hon. gentleman as heretofore expressed that this parliament should bind the hands of future parliaments. I am quite aware of the fact that it would be quite competent for succeeding parliaments to change that figure to forty, or to ten; they would have that power, but a vested interest is acquired when a statute of this kind is passed by parliament; the commission naturally expects that that is the end of it.
May I point this out to my right hon. friend: He said that a succeeding parliament could change the figure. I say that a succeeding House of Commons, of a political complexion different from that of the present, could not, if my right hon. friend's friends in the Senate wished to prevent them from so doing, alter this statute relating to the tariff -not until the political complexion of the other chamber also changed. My right hon. friend continues:
I suggest that instead of making provision for thirty years we endeavour to deal with this matter during the lifetime of a parliament. It is true that one or two sessions of this parlia-

ment will have passed, but I think the right hon. gentleman would be quite within the general constitutional practice if he said, "I desire that a given sum shall be available for this commission during the lifetime of the parliament over which I am the directing head." But when you ask parliament to bind its hands for thirty years I cannot help but think that is going too far, and that it is not quite consistent with the general principles under which we conduct our government.
After listening to my right hon. friend the government decided to change to fifteen years instead of thirty, the period during which the appropriation to the Federal District Commission should be made. The bill came before the house again on April 26, 1928, and on the motion for third reading the hon. member for Lincoln moved an amendment. His words are to be found at page 2397 of Hansard of April 26, 1928, as follows:
Mr. Speaker, I had hoped that in respect to this bill the Prime Minister would have accepted the proposal of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) to limit the period during which the annual payments are to be made to five years instead of fifteen. My chief objection to the bill is that this parliament through a commission, is making commitments for fifteen years vdiich in the ordinary course of events will cover the lifetime of possibly three, if not four parliaments. I think the principle is wrong, and I am surprised that it should be seriously proposed, especially after what the Prime Minister said in this house when in opposition and since he became head of the government.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: Did my right hon. friend follow the advice?

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: To give to a commission the expenditure of moneys over a period of fifteen years is to my mind proposterous, and to take away from future parliaments the right to say how that money shall be spent, I think is also preposterous. Therefore, I move an amendment as follow's, seconded by Mr. Manion.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
I should like to ask my
right hon. friend the leader of the opposition if he followed that advice?

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: At the moment I cannot say whether I did or not. Whether I did or did not, however, could not alter the principle which at that time my hon. friend laid down, nor would it affect the present situation.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: Absolutely true, but why quote it now?

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: I am quoting the principle which my hon. friend then laid down as the only right principle where the matter is one which may affect policy.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
My right hon. friend does not follow it.

Tariff Board-Mr. Mackenzie King

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
I have not
said we do not follow it. I shall now read the amendment.
That the bill be not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to committee of the whole with instructions that they have power to amend by striking out the word "fifteen" in line eighteen and substituting the word "five" therefor.
My right hon. friend who is now Prime Minister was not content with having laid down a principle on the second reading. After the hon. member for Lincoln had spoken the present Prime Minister again asserted the principle that should govern. I am directing my remarks to the principle which should govern as respects the bill now before the house.
On the third reading of the bill my right hon. friend's remarks are quoted at pages 2399 and 2400 of Hansard as follows:
Personally I have held a very strong view for some considerable time as to the undesirability of any legislature or parliament tying the hands of succeeding legislatures or parliaments with respect to annual expenditures.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
My right hon. friend now says, "Hear, hear." The quotation from Hansard continues:
That idea may or may not be sound.
Is my right hon. friend going to quibble? Does he say that the expenditure in connection with the proposed tariff board will not be annual? We shall have to vote annually the moneys for the purposes of carrying on the tariff board. I submit that a quibble of that nature is not worthy of him. Here it is not only expenditures but powers which are involved. Let me repeat what he said:
Personally I have had a very strong view for some considerable time as to the undesirability of any legislature or parliament tying the hands of succeeding legislatures or parliaments with respect to annual expenditures. That idea may or may not be sound, but I do not think that when matters of policy are affected-and matters of policy always are affected in relation to grants of public moneys-this parliament should tie the hands of two or three succeeding parliaments.
I direct the attention of my right hon. friend to his own words.
.... when matters of policy are affected- and matters of policy always are affected in relation to grants of public moneys-this parliament should tie the hands of two or three succeeding parliaments. Not denying that parliament has always the right to repeal legislation, I submit that it is undesirable to create vested rights with respect to legislation; and the undesirability of such a policy can never be more apparent than it is in this particular measure.
Then my right hon. friend said:
I cannot but think that the principle involved-the principle which the right hon. gentleman when in opposition always contended should be applied-is the soundest possible principle with respect to the expenditure of public money. No parliament should create a condition which leaves a succeeding parliament under the necessity of either repealing existing legislation with respect to which vested interests or rights may have arisen, or of carrying on regardless of the views of that succeeding parliament, simply because the preceding government has done what is being done in this case.
In conclusion my right hon. friend said:
As I say, it is with regret that one has to deal with this matter as a matter of principle with respect to this particular legislation, and I have endeavoured to assure the Prime Minister that it is because -we believe a principle should be laid down which will be of very great value in this country at this time, when there is a tendency to entrust public moneys in large sums to commissions, that we are impelled by whatever sense of duty may actuate us in the discharge of our obligations here to move this amendment to the third reading of the bill.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: Did not the right hon. gentleman then assert a principle contrary to what he is advocating to-day?

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: No, he did not do anything of the kind. My right hon. friend was good enough to say that when in opposition I advocated the principle I am now advocating.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: But what was the principle advocated by my right hon. friend on that occasion: I remember the debate.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: At that tame, in fact, no question of policy was involved. May I invite the attention of hon. members to what occasioned these strong declarations of principle. At that time there was under consideration the question of the appropriation of a sum of money for the purpose of maintaining under the Federal District Commission certain improvements in the city of Ottawa, expenditures which as a matter of course would be made year after year.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: Not wholly for maintenance.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
That statement of principle was not made in connection with tariffs, which after all is one of the most controversial and most important questions affecting the life of a nation. At that time my right hon. friend made his statement of principle on a matter of a comparatively trivial nature, that of voting a certain lump sum of money for a period of years for work which in the very nature of things would be



Tariff Board-Mr. Mackenzie King
carried on for years to come and which did not involve far-reaching policy, if policy at all, in any way. At the present time however my right hon. friend seeks to deny effect being given to the will of the people with respect to their decision on a question of policy affecting the tariff and failing support of himself at a general election to make it impossible for that will to be carried out after he himself may be out of office. I say it is an entirely wrong principle and I shall state the true position very frankly to my right hon. friend. No parliament or no government has the right with respect to any fiscal question to seek to bind any subsequent parliament or subsequent government. I do not think a sounder principle than that can be stated, nor can it be denied. No parliament or government has the right to bind a subsequent parliament or government with respect to fiscal matters. The taxing power whether it be in relation to the tariff or other forms of taxation belongs to those whom the people send to represent them in the House of Commons, and this right cannot be cuntailed by any parliament or government as respects its successor. In the case of a succeeding parliament there is the possibility that the same administration may be returned to office. In such a case the seriousness of a succeeding parliament being bound to a particular course of action is not so great. But when there will be -and there certainly will be-in the next election a tariff issue, for the government of the day to attempt as respects matters affecting tariff policy in a vital way to bind a subsequent government, regardless of what the will of the people as expressed in an election may be, is an action of the most arbitrary character conceivable.
I ask my right hon. friend and hon. gentlemen opposite to be just in a matter of this kind1. The amendment does not say, "You shall not have the right to appoint whatever kind of board you please, and you shall not have the right to give to that board whatever powers you please to carry out your policy." On the contrary the amendment says, in effect, "You may have all these things for the time you are in office, but do not attempt to shackle and manacle future parliaments and future administrations by making it impossible for future parliaments or administrations to change the law, as will be the case under this legislation even should the will of the people as expressed at the polls give a mandate for (the repeal of legislation of the kind."
May I say to my right hon. friend-and he should know this-that regardless of his legislation, the Liberal administration when returned to power will not be bound by any

such provisions as those he is now attempting to place in the act, if it has reason not to have confidence in those who constitute the tribunal he is attempting to form. I do not wish to reflect on any gentleman who may be named as members of the tariff board. If those gentlemen are anxious to be impartial and to be fair, I think they themselves would prefer that their tenure of office would be "at pleasure" instead of fixed for a period of ten years. If the members of the tariff board prove to be fair and impartial, I venture to say that a succeeding government might be very glad to avail itself of their services. But a sueeedang government could not be expected to avail itself of the services of those whom it does not feel it can trust, in whose judgment it has no confidence, who it knows take a point of view entirely opposed to that which it entertains. Any government holding such an opinion of its advisers could not be expected to retain them in office for one minute. What would be said of the executive itself were it to seek to retain office without having the support and confidence of the members who sit behind it? If it is necessary for the government of the day to have the support and confidence of a majority in the House of Commons, surely it is equally necessary for the government of the day that has to do with the presenting of policies to parliament to have the fullest confidence of the body which is advising them on matters pertaining to its particular policies. I say if a body of the kind were forced upon a subsequent administration, that administration would be justified in not voting the salaries of its personnel. I think this is the time to make that clear, and I hope that any person who accepts a position on this board, in the event of the legislation passing in its present form, will realize that should there be a change of administration and a Liberal government come into office, and the members of the board not enjoy its confidence, they may expect to find their term of office terminated by no salaries being voted. That apparently is the only way in which the rights of the people can be upheld in this matter as it now stands; and I say to my right hon. friend that when he, as Prime Minister, seeks to usurp the rights of the people of this country by dictating as to what body Shall govern in respect of any matters pertaining to tariff and taxation, he is going back to a period in history which some day, not very far distant, he will learn the people have not forgotten, even if he himself has.
May I say to my right hon. friend that I think he would be well-advised to follow some of the advice which his own Minister

Tariff Board-Mr. Manion
of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) has been giving at the expense of the treasury to the people of this country. We were reviewing the other evening a series of letters sent out to the press of Canada in the nature of what is called an "advertising campaign," all of which was paid for out of the treasury, and all of which was intended to further the protectionist policy of this administration. One of these letters was headed "Remember the golden rule." I wonder if my right hon. friend recalls that rule. He was at one time, I believe, a Sunday school teacher-he has not lost all his capacity for preaching even yet-and I give him credit, as I always do, for being sincere. Therefore, I ask him: Won't he remember the golden rule and apply it in this matter that affects so vitally the well-being of the people, which bears so directly on how they are to be taxed through the tariff? Let him do unto others as he would that they should do unto him, and as, in fact, they are doing unto him. We are allowing him to have hds tariff board, to shape it in the way he pleases, to give to it whatever powers he pleases. All we ask is that he shall see to it that the appointees to this board be not appointed for a decade, but that the appointment be at pleasure, so that if the board does not merit the confidence of another administration, that administration will not be bound to retain its services for purposes of advice on tariff matters and for the interpretation of tariff laws, orders in council and regulations governing the administration of customs in our land.
May I conclude what I have to say by again drawing the attention of hon. members from whatever part of the country they come to their responsibility with respect to this legislation, if they undertake in this parliament at this time to seek to bind subsequent parliaments and subsequent governments with respect to what shall be determined in matters of fiscal policy. The people have the right to tax themselves as they please through their representatives in parliament, and any administration that seeks to take away from the people's representatives in parliament their rights to determine what taxes shall be imposed through the tariff, is usurping the most essential of the powers and functions of responsible government.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

This afternoon I listened with a great deal of interest to the speech of the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King). It was a long speech; in fact the right hon. gentleman seems to be developing the habit of making long speeches He has made three set speeches this year, one lasting for three and a half hours, one for four and a half hours and the speech this afternoon taking a little over two hours, if I noticed the clock correctly when he rose. I do not like to see him setting a bad example like that, particularly to the younger members of the house. I believe his speech this afternoon would have been very much better had he boiled down his argument and taken a shorter time, and naturally I like to see him make a good speech.
During the time he spoke he used some words which I do not think were quite proper. He said on one occasion that my right hon. leader (Mr. Bennett) had some ulterior motive in introducing this legislation. subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
I know of no reason why, if we wanted only to further our views, we should have appointed a board of any kind. We might just as well have done it without appointing a board at all. That would have been more logical, more sensible and more straightforward; it would have been the right attitude to take if we only wanted to further our views. But by appointing this board it is obvious we are acting in the interests of the people in general and for the purpose of getting the facts and submitting them to the people and to the parliament of Canada.
The right hon. leader of the opposition continually takes an attitude in this house which seems to indicate that he has forgotten that there was an election a iittle less than a year ago, by which he was asked, very politely but very emphatically, to retire. He rises in the house continually and speaks as though he thinks he is speaking for the people of this country. With all due deference, I submit that my right hon. leader speaks for the people of this country at the present time.
Then the right hon. gentleman spoke of secret hearings; he said that these hearings were to be secret, and he emphasized that point rather strongly. However, it is obvious from a reading of the bill that the hearings are not to be in secret; in no place does it say they are. It does state that certain information will be considered confidential, and rightly so. If you are to go into the internal business affairs of manufacturing or producing corporations of any kind, that information should not be broadcast. Take the wheat pool, for example; if we wished to go into their affairs for some reason or other, or if the government inquired into the internal affairs and confidential matters of any other corporation, that information should be kept confidential and should not be given to others competing in the same fields. Section 6 reads:
Whenever a report has been made under this act, a copy thereof and a copy of the evidence, if any, taken, and of the information obtained (except such evidence and information as was of a confidential character under subsection ten of section five hereof) in connection there-

with shall be laid before parliament by the minister fifteen days after the opening of the next session thereafter, or within fifteen days after the making of the report if parliament is then in session.
In other words, there is nothing secret about this board or its action.
The right hon. member dealt with many details of this legislation which I think might well have been left until the bill was being considered in committee of the whole. So far as his remarks are concerned, may I say that to my mind he simply put up a number of straw men in order to be able to knock them down. He took the attitude of supporting the much abused and oppressed common people who he apparently felt were dependent wholly upon him. He would not permit our so-called "vicious" attempts to interfere with their rights and to wipe out all forms of democracy. He would demolish this attempt of ours which has never taken place. After all, this legislation is not like the laws of the Medes and Persians; if there are changes needed later on, those changes can be made. This legislation can be amended at the proper time and on the proper occasion, if it is found that certain portions of it are not working out as expected.
In his very excellent speech the hon. member for Hants-Kings (Mr. Ilsley) admitted, as did his right hon. leader, that some kind of tariff board is required in this country, and apparently it is only as to the form of the board that there is disagreement. A tariff board of some kind is required to assist ministers of finance. Any hon. member who has been in this house for some years will realize that a minister of finance has not the time or opportunity to go into all the details of a tariff-or to deal with those details as they should be dealt with. He must have some form of fact finding board to help him come to proper conclusions.
The purpose of this board is to obtain facts and to lay those facts not only before the Minister of Finance and the government but before the parliament of Canada. No one will suggest that any government can evade the responsibility of making a tariff for this country. No matter what government is in power, whether it be the present government or the government of my right hon. friend, that government must take the responsibility of whatever tariff changes are made. That responsibility cannot be transferred to any board. The hon. member for Hants-Kings said that this board would "dictate" to the government, but I do not think there is any indication that such will be the case. I do not think this proposed legislation would permit the board to dictate to the government
Tariff Board-Mr. Manion
of my right hon. friend if he should come back into power a few years hence. It is a fact finding and advisory board entirely.
As was so well stated by my right horn leader, another function of this board will be to compare the costs of production in Canada with the costs prevailing in other countries. It has been pointed out already that it may be very difficult to get the actual' facts, but it should be easy to obtain approximate comparisons. For example, one would not need to be a great economist to know that when Russia is paying wages of $30 per month-there are a few exceptions in the case of experts from outside-and then takes back from the worker much of that wage for different purposes, leaving probably only two-thirds, Russia can produce much cheaper than those countries in which high wages and high standards of living prevail. By the way, I noticed a rather interesting statement in the Montreal Star of Saturday evening, to the effect that the United States is working out a method whereby on January 1 next they will put on a watertight embargo against goods from Russia.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
They
turned down the hon. gentleman's government on that, did they not?

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
I do not think they had an opportunity of either turning us down or putting us up. That policy proves to a large extent the rightness of the policy adopted 'by this government in regard to Russia. The reason the United States is taking this stand is because they have discovered that the cost of production in the Union of Soviet Socialistic Republics is based upon practical slavery or prison labour. The United States have found that they cannot compete with that type of production and keep up their own Standard of living.
As we all know, there are still other countries which can produce very cheaply. One does not need to be a great economist to know that proper tariffs are necessary in order to compete with some of the central European countries. Japan is another example ; she can produce some goods at a much lower cost than Canada, and unless we wish to lower our standard of living by lowering the rates of wages, there is no possibility of our competing with them. Therefore, it is a simple matter to compare, at least approximately, the costs of production in other countries with those of Canada.
I have been a member of this house for some years and it appears to me that in the past the tariff has been worked out too much on the hit and miss principle. Such was as
Tariff Board-Mr. Manion

clearly the case when my right hon. friend was in power, because for one year at least, from 1925 to 1928, he was forced to depend upon the Progressive group as to whether or not he would stay in power. It was certainly hit and miss during those days. In the past it has been a question of deputations, and pressure of various kinds being put upon the government in power. Every government is affected to a certain extent by the pressure of the representations made, and I believe that a tariff board is absolutely necessary in a country such as Canada where the two major parties believe in a protective policy. The only difference of opinion is as to the degree of protection.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: In some cases it is a question of expediency.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: The hon. member for East Essex (Mr. Morand) states that in some cases it is a question of expediency. No doubt that was the case when my right hon. friend was leading a minority group and holding power with the support of the other minority groups in the house.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: The hon. member should speak for himself.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
May I suggest to my hon. friend that he follow his own advice. There is no other hon. member in this house-I say this in a friendly spirit-who so often speaks for others while they are speaking.
The Conservative party was elected because of its protectionist principles. Those principles were advocated from end to end of Canada during the last elections, as well as during every other campaign since I have been a member of this house, and I have been here during the last five campaigns. We sincerely believe that the protectionist policy is the only policy which will permit this country to compete with other countries of the world. Believing that, we should not appoint absolute free traders as members of this board. Such a procedure would be most-illogical.
During the previous discussion on this bill, the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) stated that protection was of no use to the mixed farmer. While listening to her remarks I came to the conclusion that she was the one who was mixed, and not the farmer, because if there is any farmer in the world who benefits from a protectionist policy, it is the farmer who goes in for mixed farming. That is well illustrated by the farmers of Quebec around the cities nf Montreal, Sherbrooke and other great
XMr. Manion.]
manufacturing centres and by the farmers of Ontario around Toronto, Hamilton and other cities of that sort. I will admit quite freely that the wheat farmer of the west is not protected to a very great extent.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: I admit that-quite freely; he is the most difficult man to assist, but in his case we have done what my hon. friend's leader never did. Although he was in power for ten years and although he carried out the protectionist principle at all times, he did nothing to assist the wheat growers of the west, whereas my right hon. leader at this very session of the house is introducing legislation to help the wheat growers of the west by assistance of five cents per bushel.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
My hon. friends opposite
laugh, but I defy any hon. member on that side from the prairie provinces to rise in his place and disown or oppose this five cents per bushel assistance to the wheat farmers of the west. I notice they wander around the question; they skid along on thin ice fairly often, but not one of them has risen to oppose it.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
I hope the Minister of
Railways will not take in too much territory in that challenge.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
I take in every portion of
the three prairie provinces. By the way, when my hon. friend was speaking on this question some time ago, I asked him if he were opposed to this five cent policy and he rose in anger and asked me what right I had to put such a question to him.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: The Minister of Railways does not know himself what the five cents per bushel on wheat means.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: The Minister of Railways does, and I challenge my hon. friend right now to say whether he is opposed to that policy of giving assistance to the wheat farmer.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: I certainly can oppose it as a barley grower. What do I get for barley growing?

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
What about the wheat
grower?

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
What does this five
cents per bushel mean?

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
Will the Minister of
Railways tell me what it means?

Tariff Board-Mr. Manion

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
I am not discussing that
question at length. I could discuss that very quickly, but I have only forty minutes. I have not as much time as my hon. friend's leader had when he was speaking. When the time comes, it will be explained to the house in full.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: Will my hon. friend permit a question?

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
Is this five
cent bonus-

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: Sit down.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
The minister
has allowed me to ask a question, and it is a reasonable one. Is this a sectional proposition? Does it apply only to the west or does it apply to Ontario and Quebec as well?

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
It applies to the wheat
growers of this country.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: Will my hon. friend kindly explain how the five cents per bushel rebate in the freight rate on wheat will be passed on to the farmer, and how the farmer can get this five cents per bushel?

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
I am not dealing with that at length at the moment. I have yet to finish my speech on the tariff board legislation, and I do not intend to be drawn away from my subject by my hon. friends, not one of whom has had the courage to rise and oppose this five cent per bushel policy with respect to wheat.
It is quite true the farmers of Canada have been hit by present conditions; no one disputes that. But the manufacturers have been hit; the transportation companies have been hit; all classes have been hit just as all classes throughout the world have been affected, because a world condition exists over which we have no control. We cannot control to any great extent the injury that is being done to the farmer by the present world situation. When it changes, the policies that we have brought in since my right hon. leader came into power will doubtless show their beneficial effects.
Another statement made by some of those who were speaking against the tariff board was that the protectionist policy is for the purpose of stopping trade between Canada and other countries. That is simply another ridiculous statement, because nobody wants to stop trade between this and any other country. What we do, and I think wisely, is to advise that as far as possible the people of
Canada shall produce what they can economically produce. That is the attitude we take. The fact for example that Germany before the war was the most highly protected country in the world and was rapidly overtaking all the other countries in international trade shows that protection does not interfere with world trade. Even at the present time, with conditions bad as they are throughout the world, Germany, France and the United States, the three most highly protected countries in the world, have very large world trade.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: What about unemployment?

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
Free trade England has
the worst unemployment situation in the world.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: No.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
My hon. friends opposite
always forget that the really profitable trade to any country is that carried on amongst the people themselves, the home trade; the ability to buy and sell among themselves is at any time the greatest proof of the prosperity of any country. The trouble with too many who are out and out free traders-and there are not many opposite me at present-* is that they veer too strongly toward theories and too little toward facts. They argue theoretically, and on theoretical grounds alone a good case could no doubt be made out for free trade, but unfortunately the facts do not agree with the theories, and whenever they find that to be the case they say: So much the worse for the facts. That is the position taken by my hon. friends opposite. When the facts disagree with the theories, they simply ignore the facts.
My hon. friends opposite have at all times on public platforms and in budget debates stated that we stand for higher and liigher protection. We do not stand for any such thing. I believe in protection, but I believe protection, just like anything else, can be carried too far.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: How far?

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
Well, as far as we are
carrying it is the right distance. I do not believe in higher and higher tariffs; I believe in fairer and fairer trade. I believe in giving our producers in this country an opportunity to produce on a fair basis of competition with those of other countries. Even free trade England is realizing that she cannot compete, and she introduced the safeguarding of industries duty to show she could protect some of her industries. I venture to assert that
Tariff Board-Mr. Manion

within the next two or three years England will be adopting the same type of protection as other countries have adopted.
This legislation is not an attempt to give to my right hon. leader or the government any such powers as are at present possessed by the United States. The United States has the power practically overnight to raise the tariff by 50 per cent and in some cases, 1 believe, to a greater degree.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
So can
the present government.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
Yes, in the regulation of
dumping, but not in other ways. During the last election I remember going into a little town in western Canada that is dependent upon a craft paper mill. The manager of that mill told me that within recent months he had obtained in Minneapolis a good order, an order for a couple of carloads of craft paper and he had shipped it to that city. He informed me he was immediately asked by the tariff board of the United States to appear before them and give reasons why he had a right to ship that into the United States. It is true he might have said that he would not appear, because he was operating in a Canadian town, but had he not gone that would have been a reason for the tariff board to bar him out. He appeared before them and they made conditions so unpleasant for him that he told me he had never attempted to get another order from the United States and he never would. We have no intention of taking any such powers as that under this board. We will appoint a board which is a fact finding board for the Finance Minister, the government and parliament in general.
I should like to discuss another point before I resume my seat, and that is the question of the ten year appointment. I suppose a large proportion of the objection to this measure is to the members of this board being appointed for a term of ten years. But if you are going to secure men for a board of this kind, you can get them only by giving them an appointment for a reasonable period. The old tariff board is a good illustration of the way the personnel of such a board changes when the appointments are not for any specified time of a reasonable length. Mr. Graham was a member of the board for only a short time, and then he retired. Mr. Lambert was a member for only a short time and then he retired. Mr. Moore retired, and Mr. McKenzie retired. These come to my mind at the moment; I do not know what other retirements there were, but it seemed to me that the board was not stable enough

to be of any use to any government, even to the government of my right hon. friend opposite. I will go further. Recently when we had to appoint, under the legislation of the house, a pension appeal board, we found very great difficulty, because of the indefinite term and the low salary, in getting a good man to take over the chairmanship. I say that quite frankly. We have different commissions in this country, the members of which are appointed for ten years or longer. The members of the railway commission are appointed for ten years, and speaking of the railway commissioners, when we oame into power nearly all the members of the board were appointees of my right hon. friend. Suppose we took the attitude that he took this afternoon, that we would not stand by a board that he had appointed.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: You retired some of them.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: We did not. A number of them resigned of their own free will. In fact, we could not have crowded them into resigning.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: All judges are appointed for life. They are not in politics.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
But the Board of Railway Commissioners is a commission. The members of the Farm Loan Board are appointed for ten years. Judges, as my hon. friend from Sheiburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) says, are appointed for life, and I say because they are appointed for life, because they are independent of the comings and goings of governments, we have one of the finest judiciaries in the world. The judges also retire on a pension, as is provided in this bill. In addition, the fact of appointing the board for ten years makes the board more independent and brings about the very object which my right hon. friend says he desires. It puts them in a position to be independent, not only of the incoming government, but also of the government which appointed them, because there will be at least one election, and probably two, before their term expires.
Another reason for the ten year appointment is that it gives stability not only to the board, but also to tariffs, when you have such a board going into all the details of the tariff question and advising the Minister of Finance and the government. Finally, it makes the board more or less non-partisan. My right hon. -friend the leader of the opposition would not say that he ever appointed any Conservatives to the bench. There are none that I know of.

Tariff Board-Mr. Manion

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: My right hon. friend cannot name very many. Perhaps he is going to name one. He rose as if he were going to do so, but he has not done so, and I venture to say that if he can name one, that is the limit. I do not think he ever did appoint anybody not of his own political faith.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Justice
Newcombe was one of the first judicial appointments we made. He was appointed to the supreme court, and he was a Conservative.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: I have not the least idea what his politics are, but he had been Deputy Minister of Justice for a long time.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: I think he is a Tory.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: He had been Deputy Minister of Justice for many years, for thirty years, I am told. I say that my right hon. friend has appointed to the bench, practically always, men of his own political faith, and I offer no criticism of that. We do the same, generally speaking, on our side of the house, but neither he nor anyone else would say that the men appointed as judges, generally speaking, are anything but non-partisan, and there is no reason in the world why the members of this tariff board, appointed as they will be for ten years, should not be just as non-partisan as the judiciary.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: May I ask a question? My hon. friend was appointed a member of the Ontario Liquor Control Board. Was he appointed for ten years?

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: No, but I could have stayed for ten years had I chose. I chose to resign. I was appointed for as long as I chose to remain, and I could have been there yet. My hon. friend will not deny that.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: I do not know.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: I do. That is the difference.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: What about the Clerk of the House? Was he a Grit? We appointed him. He is a Tory, and he is a good man.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: I do not think he is a Tory. I think he is independent. I see my time is about up.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: I would ask lion, gentlemen to desist from loud remarks and interruptions while the minister is speaking. He has only ten minutes left, and a member cannot present his case when he is continually interrupted.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: Especially when they are speaking from the other side.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: I resent that, The hon. member has no right to make any such statement.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: Withdraw.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: I am not going to take it back either.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman would be well advised to withdraw the observation he has just made. It reflects upon the institutions of this country, and I think-after a moment's reflection he will realize that it is unwise to charge the Speaker with partiality in the terms that he has used. I trust that he will withdraw.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: I have heard the Prime Minister do the same thing that I have done, reflect on the Speaker.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: It is a matter for the Speaker himself. He is the servant of the house, and he can only discharge his duties as the servant of the house if the house gives him its support. When an hon. member of this house makes an aspersion of the kind my hon. friend used, without any justification in fact, and then says he is not going to withdraw the expression, I think, Mr. Speaker, that the house will have to take cognizance of it and deal with it in another way.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: Go ahead and deal with it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: I will make the motion to-morrow.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
I was going to conclude
by saying that, due to the fact that the board will be appointed for a period of ten years, the tendency will be for the board to be a more scientific body in regard to gathering and presenting data to the government under which it will serve.
The objects of the board are clearly set forth in the explanatory notes, and I will conclude my remarks by quoting two or three sentences from them, which will lay before the house in a proper manner the purpose of the board:
The intention is to secure, as a result of the work of the board, a constantly increasing body of information which will be of service to the government and to parliament.
The duties of the board are set out in section 4 of the bill. As directed by the minister, they are to inquire into the price and cost of raw' materials, the cost of transportation, the cost of production, the cost, efficiency and conditions of labour, the prices received by producers, etc., in Canada or elsewhere, and all conditions and factors affecting cost of production and price to the consumers in Canada, and
3162	COMMONS
Tariff Board-Mr. Stewart (Edmonton)
as compared with other countries. The board is empowered to make inquiry into any other matter upon which the minister desires information, in relation to any goods which if brought into Canada or produced in Canada are subject to or exempt from duties of customs or excise.
That is very clear; the purpose of the board is to act as a fact finding advisory commission. The right hon. leader of the government is to be congratulated by the parliament of Canada for bringing in legislation to constitute this board, and he will be congratulated also, I submit, by the people of Canada.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: I do not rise, Mr. Speaker, to object to the appointment of a tariff board. I believe that a tariff board acting in an advisory capacity can 'be very helpful to any government. I think there is no dispute about that. Nor do I intend to go into the provisions of the present bill in detail. That has been very well done already by the hon. member for Hants-Kings (Mr. Ilsley), and later this afternoon by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King). I do not intend to say very much in regard to the remarks of the hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) because I do not think that more than ten per cent of them were relevant to the question before the house. If we are going to have a tariff debate I am ready to take part in it any day, but no doubt many of these tariff matters will be discussed when the tariff resolutions are before us for consideration, and we shall then have an opportunity of expressing our views in that regard.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: I brought in the tariff only because my hon. friends had referred to it, and I was replying to their arguments.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
I am making no objections to the hon. gentleman's speech. I am simply stating that for the most part his remarks were irrelevant to the question before the house.
Having said that we all appear to be in favour of an advisory board on tariff and taxation, it then becomes a question of method. May I say that so far as I am concerned I find no fault with the leader of the government for abolishing the old tariff board, whether there was only one member then existent, or two, or how many there were. Clearly in my opinion that board, as political questions are discussed and party alignments are known in Canada, would have been of little or no service to the presept government. Moreover the present government was elected on the specific promise to

increase tariffs. They have a mandate to carry out their promise. I wish however to take issue with my.hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals when he states that the party to which he belongs is speaking for the whole of the Canadian people. There is always an opposition, and when my hon. friend was over here he spoke in no uncertain terms when voicing his opinions on public matters. We ought to remember that the majority of hon. members who sit on that side of the house procured in the last election about 200,000 votes more than the Liberal party. In voting strength therefore they do not in such a large way represent the public opinion in Canada. It is our duty to represent what we believe and what as a party we espouse; it is our duty as an opposition to state our policy.
For the last forty years I can think of no issue which has held such an important place in Canadian politics as the tariff. It has been one of the vital questions upon which different parliaments have divided upon every occasion. A board to be set up for the purpose of advising upon tariff matters must of necessity, in my opinion, be a board who feel and think the same as the party in power. I can conceive of no other condition, and I find no fault with the action of the government in proposing to set up the board. I complain only of the method they are adopting.
To my mind there are some provisions in the bill now before the house which will cause the government considerable difficulty. I should like to direct the attention of hon. members to a provision in clause 4 of the bill in which it is pointed out that the board will advise on certain particulars respecting rates to be charged. I sincerely trust the government will see fit to delete that clause from the bill. To my mind no board has the right to dictate rates to the government of Canada, the body which alone is directly responsible to the people. A board may find facts and may bring the necessary information before the Minister of Finance; he in turn may discuss them with the members of the government, who may make up their minds, as to the necessary rates.
The complaint has been made that the late government did not have information before them. Where did the present government get the information whereby they have at this moment-or will have when the tariff items are passed by this house-amended over one-half the items of the whole tariff schedule? Where did they get that information? Moreover I will say that the most important items entering into the livelihood of the people

Tariff Board-Mr. Stewart (Edmonton)
of Canada are to be changed by the Minister of Finance and his government without a tittle of information except what they may have gained behind closed doors. I will admit there was a hearing where representations might be made, and as a spectator I took occasion to attend. Not one word of information was forthcoming however as to what was to be done. We were informed that briefs were filed, and action was to be taken upon those briefs. So far as the public were concerned however until the day the right hon. Minister of Finance brought down his budget certainly no hon. member on this side of the house and probably very few on that side knew what the changes would be. I say if the government is willing to take the responsibility for making these drastic changes, which in many instances mean complete exclusion of particular articles so far as trade is concerned, all I have to say is that from the point of view of the government there does not appear to be any necessity for a tariff board. I am not going to offer any complaint on that score; theirs is the responsibility. They said they would assume that responsibility; the people accepted their offer and placed them in power, and they are now in a position where they are responsible for the changes the bill now before us would involve.
Having voiced my opinion I now claim exactly the same measure of responsibility for the party to which I belong. I do not represent a high tariff party, but rather the opposite. If the party which I support are fortunate enough to succeed in the next election I do not wish to be handicapped by being advised by a group of gentlemen who were selected because on a question of national importance they were diametrically opposed to my views. I think I heard one of my hon. friends say that there is no chance. All I have to say to him is that he has not been travelling in recent weeks.
My objections to the bill now before us are twofold. First, the suggested term of ten years is an imposition upon any government which might follow the present one. I make this statement because with respect to the board which has been dismissed, I stand firmly behind the action of the present Prime Minister. Moreover may I add that I do not see the slightest necessity for establishing a tariff board by legislative action. After all the government must take responsibility in choosing advisers, and I wonder why they want by statute to fasten for ten years upon the parliament of Canada gentlemen who hold their point of view. My hon. friend the
Minister of Railways and Canals, and indeed the Minister of Finance himself, made the statement the other day that the tariff board would be no different from the Board of Railway Commissioners. I think that was an absurd statement to make, the worst kind of absurdity.

speechtext:
Not so far as I know. If my hon. friend has any information on the point I should like to have it. My understanding is that the duties of the Board of Railway Commissioners are purely and simply to adjudicate upon rates. I do not view the Board of Railway Commissioners in the same light as I would view the tariff board at all. As for making comparison with the appointment of judges, may I say that I have known some judges who were at one time my political opponents, and yet they have made some of the best judges who have been placed upon the bench. I am frank enough to say that I have never been able to discover that they were in the slightest degree biased, even in political matters. But the matter now before us is of an entirely different nature. No doubt we will have to stand for the setting up of the proposed board by statute, I most emphatically resent the fastening of a board of this character upon future parliaments. May I repeat however that I see no necessity for a statute. I take it that the board is bound to be political in character. If the people of Canada decide that they wish to have a high tariff government, they have a right to their decision and we must be prepared to accept the high tariff policy. If, on the other hand the people of Canada decide the opposite, then they should not be advised by a board such as the one proposed, and when that occasion arose the proper thing to do would be to discharge that board at once and appoint one in keeping with the viewpoint of
3164	COMMONS
Tariff Board-Mr. Stewart (Edmonton)
the party in office. That, however, is a matter which is immaterial to me, because I am bound to say-and I think my prediction will be borne out before the board is in operation very long-that upon any occasion when the board is asked to report on rates to be fixed nothing but trouble will result for the government. The responsibility of fixing rates rests with the government, and with the government alone.
May I say in a general way that I for one am not very much enamoured of this commission business. Just recently the government appointed a commission, and that commission has not helped them very much. We had a few commissions in our time that did not make the work of administration very easy for us. I am convinced that the old and well-tried principle of governmental responsibility is the best principle in the long run. Commissions may recommend policies to the government, but they arc not responsible for the putting of those policies into effect, and the adoption of such policies almost inevitably tends to place the government in a difficult position.
In conclusion I desire to reiterate, that I am opposing the bill because of its arbitrary provisions, and I am opposing it because of the clause making the tenure of the commissioners ten years. With those clauses withdrawn, I am prepared to support the bill. So far as I am concerned, I say emphatically that I do not propose again at any time to lend my voice in support of any commission or body of men whose duty it shall be to advise the government definitely as to what action shall be taken in respect to any particular matter. I repeat, 1 believe in the old system of governmental responsibility.
